title: When the Count Could Not Describe the Pain
source: Published author's essay The Life Between Diagnoses, editorial revision 15 Oct 2026

scenes.text: There were mornings when even water refused to stay down. A blood count might describe part of the illness. It could not describe that morning.
I finished high school at sixteen. My father had died, and illness had already interrupted much of my last year. I still graduated, but not with the results I needed for medical school.
The examination paper recorded the marks accurately. It did not record the hospital days behind them. I wanted to study medicine. Instead, I was learning what it meant to be a patient.
Doctors and medical students found my case interesting. I understood why they needed to ask questions. I also learned that the patient remains when the students leave the room.
I began to recognize a flare before any laboratory report appeared. That was not a diagnostic talent. It was experience purchased through too many difficult days.
Eventually I studied chemistry. It became work I cared deeply about, not a prize that illness had thoughtfully chosen for me. There were experiments and questions I wanted to pursue on my own terms.
A week before travelling to the United States, another attack meant an endoscopy and treatment. I wanted to think about the journey. My body had other plans.
Over time I learned the pharmacology of treatments that could help and could also create their own burdens. Understanding their mechanisms did not make the decisions simple.
As a researcher, I know the value of measurements. Yet a blood count, a biopsy, and the ability to drink water answer different questions. None cancels the others.
I do not want my life reduced to a laboratory result, or the illness turned into a lesson I was meant to learn. I want the ordinary freedom to plan tomorrow without counting on it being interrupted.
